contributions.headingText: Placental site trophoblastic tumour (PSTT) is a malignant neoplasm of implantation site intermediate trophoblast.
2C75.0 & XH1RM5 Malignant trophoblastic neoplasms of placenta & Placental site trophoblastic tumour
Uterine corpus, lower uterine segment, and (rarely) in extrauterine sites {14501817}

Two thirds of the cases follow a full-term pregnancy, with a median latency of 12–18 months (ranging from a few months to 20 years) {16246400; 10329037}. Vaginal bleeding, uterine enlargement, or history of missed abortion is the most common presentation, followed by amenorrhoea and abdominal pain {16085293; 11520134; 12092014}. A mild to moderate elevation of serum hCG, of 5–26 000 mIU/mL (average: 680 mIU/mL), is detectable in 80% of cases {16246400; 11520134; 16085293; 12092014}. At presentation, > 80% of cases are FIGO stage I {16246400}. FIGO stage II commonly involves adnexa or pelvic lymph nodes. Recurrence or metastasis occurs in 25–30% of patients {11520134; 12092014}.
PSTT occurs in women ranging in age from 20 to 63 years (mean: 31 years) {16246400; 10329037; 6264815; 6200262}. It is rare, representing 0.25–5% of all trophoblastic tumours {29780773}.

PSTT arises from invasive or implantation-type, intermediate (extravillous) trophoblast {17498600}. It shows rare genetic imbalances by comparative genomic hybridization {14657956}. There is a preferential requirement of paternal X chromosome in the tumour genome {10879746; 17643092} and a female predominance {27246306}.

PSTT generally involves the endomyometrium and presents as well-circumscribed nodular masses as large as 10 cm, with a solid, fleshy, whitish-tan to light-yellow cut surface. Deep myometrial invasion is seen in 50% of the cases. Focal haemorrhage and necrosis are present in nearly half of the cases {16246400; 6200262}. Transmural invasion is seen in 10%, and perforation may occur {16246400}.

The tumour has an infiltrative growth pattern consisting of aggregates or sheets of large, polyhedral to round, predominantly mononucleated cells. Scattered multinucleated cells are common. The tumour cells typically infiltrate the myometrium by separating the smooth muscle cells. Cytologically, the cells have abundant amphophilic (and occasionally eosinophilic or clear) cytoplasm. Nuclei are pleomorphic and nuclear atypia is generally pronounced, with frequent, large, convoluted nuclei and marked hyperchromasia. Most tumours have a low mitotic count, with 1–2 mitoses/mm2 (equating to 2–4 mitoses/10 HPF of 0.5 mm in diameter and 0.2 mm2 in area) {16246400; 11192071; 6200262}. Characteristic vascular invasion is often present, in which the tumour cells replace the vascular wall of myometrial vessels. The differential diagnoses include exaggerated placental site, other trophoblastic tumours (epithelioid trophoblastic tumour and choriocarcinoma), squamous cell carcinoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, epithelioid leiomyoma, and leiomyosarcoma. Tumour cells diffusely express hPL, MUC4, HSD3B1, HLA-G, and MCAM (CD146). Expression of hCG and inhibin is more limited. Ki-67 is expressed in 10–30% of cells {17498600; 11192071}.
DNA genotyping provides a definitive diagnostic separation of placental site trophoblastic tumour from other neoplasms and may therefore be helpful {18820674; 26980014}.
Essential: an invasive trophoblastic neoplasm with compatible immunoprofile.
The FIGO and Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classifications are used for staging.

Simple hysterectomy is curative in most cases. However, approximately 25–30% of patients may develop recurrent disease or metastasis, and about half of those patients may die of the tumour {11520134; 1848895; 12092014}. The mortality rate is 6.5–27% {31047719}. Poor prognostic features include tumour cells with clear cytoplasm, deep myometrial invasion, large tumour size, necrosis, and high mitotic count (> 2.5 mitoses/mm2, equating to > 5 mitoses/10 HPF of 0.5 mm in diameter and 0.2 mm2 in area). Advanced stage, ≥ 48 months since antecedent pregnancy, age > 40 years, and the presence of tumour cells with clear cytoplasm are independent predictors of worse prognosis {16246400; 19552948; 30607597}.
